query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated predictive approach that combines CALPHAD-based high-throughput screening with machine-learning interatomic potential simulations will reliably identify high-entropy alloy compositions that exhibit significantly reduced phonon thermal conductivity. This reduction is achieved by targeting alloy systems which inherently produce high levels of atomic-scale lattice distortions and mass disorder—features that enhance phonon scattering—thus outperforming conventional empirical or first‐principles methods by at least 20% in prediction accuracy within simple, single-phase FCC or BCC alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys in a single-phase FCC or BCC structure with moderate grain sizes and minimal intermetallic precipitates.
generation.intervention: Application of the integrated predictive tool to screen potential alloy compositions followed by synthesis (e.g., using additive manufacturing or 3D ink extrusion printing) and measurement of phonon thermal conductivity under high-temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures relevant for thermal insulation applications (up to 900 °C) and conditions ensuring the maintenance of the single-phase microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale lattice distortions and mass disorder in the alloy matrix that serve as effective phonon scattering centers.
generation.mechanism: The predictive approach identifies compositions where high configurational entropy leads to significant local lattice strain and mass fluctuation. These factors enhance phonon scattering, thereby lowering the phonon thermal conductivity relative to alloys predicted by traditional methods.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys predicted by the integrated approach will exhibit phonon thermal conductivities reduced by approximately 20% or more compared to those identified via conventional prediction techniques, with experimental thermal conductivity measurements matching the computational predictions within acceptable error margins.
generation.baseline: Predictions made using conventional empirical models or first-principles calculations without high-throughput integration, which have demonstrated lower accuracy in capturing the effects of lattice distortion on phonon transport.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be valid only for high-entropy alloys that form stable single-phase FCC or BCC structures. In multiphase alloys or those with significant intermetallic precipitation, the model’s predictions may not correlate well with experimental outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in prediction accuracy and the quantitative reduction in thermal conductivity remain uncertain until comprehensive experimental validation is performed. Variations arising from processing conditions or microstructural inhomogeneities may also affect the outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize one or more high-entropy alloys identified by the predictive approach using a controlled additive manufacturing process. Measure the phonon thermal conductivity at temperatures up to 900 °C (relevant for thermal insulation applications) using a laser flash apparatus. Compare these measurements against a set of baseline alloys selected based on conventional prediction methods.
measurements: Phonon thermal conductivity across a relevant temperature range
Microstructural characterization (e.g., X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy) to confirm single-phase FCC or BCC structure
Quantification of lattice distortions via atom probe tomography or similar techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured phonon thermal conductivity of the alloys identified by the predictive approach does not show an improvement of at least ~20% reduction relative to the baseline alloys, or if significant deviations in microstructure (e.g., formation of intermetallic phases) are observed that contradict model assumptions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. The synthesized quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA shows high thermal stability in terms of grain coarsening. Even though there was an increase in the grain size during He implantation, the material preserved its nano-crystallinity and showed only approximately 10 nm change in grain size after ~8.45 at.% He implantation. The previously studied quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA demonstrated a similar thermal stability regarding grain morphology [22] . One of the properties that distinguishes this quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA from the previously studied RHEAs is the grain refinement observed during dual-beam irradiation. Grain refinement was observed before in other materials [32] . Two main suggested mechanisms are discussed in the literature: (i) defect clusters produced during irradiation can migrate to sub-grain boundaries and form cell structures that lead to small grain formation [32] and (ii) cascades that are larger than the grain size can form stacking faults across the grain breaking it into two separate crystalline structures (observed in FCC material) [33] . Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

The fields of aerospace and fossil energy have benefited from decades of the development of Ni-base superalloys. However, to obtain further efficiency gains and environmental friendliness, developing new materials with inexpensive, light, and strong characteristics is required. Numerous efforts can be found in the development of novel ferritic superalloys containing a disordered body-centered-cubic (BCC) matrix with ordered B2 and/or L2 1 precipitates due to their good creep resistance at elevated temperatures and relatively lower densities [1] , [2] . However, these emerging precipitation-strengthened ferritic alloys still face some drawbacks, such as the low high-temperature strength and not lightweight, which limit their applications. To overcome these issues, new alloy-design strategies are required. Recently, the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) or multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) has revolutionized the traditional alloy-design strategy, using multi-principal components (≥5) instead of one or two key components [3] – [10] .
